Package for \"A Study on the Pythonic Functional Constructs\u0027 Understandability\" to appear at ICSE 2024\n\n\n\nAuthors: Cyrine Zid, Fiorella Zampetti, Giuliano Antoniol, Massimiliano Di penta\n\nArticle Preprint: https://mdipenta.github.io/files/ICSE24_funcExperiment.pdf\n\nArtifacts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8191782\n\nLicense: GPL V3.0\n\n\nThis package contains folders and files with code and data used in the study described in the paper. In the following, we first provide all fields required for the submission, and then report a detailed description of all repository folders.\n\nArtifact Description\n\nPurpose\n\nThe artifact is about a controlled experiment aimed at investigating the extent to which Pythonic functional constructs have an impact on source code understandability. The artifact archive contains:\n\n\n\nThe material to allow replicating the study (see Section Experimental-Material)\n\nRaw quantitative results, working datasets, and scripts to replicate the statistical analyses reported in the paper. Specifically, the executable part of the replication package reproduces figures and tables of the quantitative analysis (RQ1 and RQ2) of the paper starting from the working datasets.\n\nSpreadsheets used for the qualitative analysis (RQ3).\n\n\nWe apply for the following badges:\n\n\n\nAvailable and reusable: because we provide all the material that can be used to replicate the experiment, but also to perform the statistical analyses and the qualitative analyses (spreadsheets, in this case)\n\n\nProvenance\n\n\n\nPaper preprint link: https://mdipenta.github.io/files/ICSE24_funcExperiment.pdf\n\nArtifacts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8191782\n\n\nData\n\nResults have been obtained by conducting the controlled experiment involving Prolificworkers as participants. Data collection and processing followed a protocol approved by the University ethical board. Note that all data enclosed in the artifact is completely anonymized and does not contain sensible information.\n\nFurther details about the provided dataset can be found in the Section Results\u0027 directory and files\n\nSetup and Usage (for executable artifacts):\n\nSee the Section Scripts to reproduce the results, and instructions for running them\n\nExperiment-Material/\n\nContains the material used for the experiment, and, specifically, the following subdirectories:\n\nGoogle-Forms/\n\nContains (as PDF documents) the questionnaires submitted to the ten experimental groups.\n\nTask-Sources/\n\nContains, for each experimental group (G-1...G-10), the sources used to produce the Google Forms, and, specifically: - The cover letter (Letter.docx). - A directory for each experimental task (Lambda 1, Lambda 2, Comp 1, Comp 2, MRF 1, MRF 2, Lambda Comparison, Comp Comparison, MRF Comparison). Each directory contains: (i) the exercise text (in both Word and .txt format), the source code snippet, and its .png image to be used in the form. Note: the \"Comparison\" tasks do not have any exercise as the purpose is always the same, i.e., to compare the (perceived) understandability of the snippets and return the results of the comparison.\n\nCode-Examples-Table1/\n\nContains the source code snippets used as objects of the study (the same you can find under \"Task-Sources/\"), named as reported in Table 1.\n\nResults\u0027 directory and files\n\n\u00a0\n\nraw-responses/\n\nContains, as spreadsheets, the raw responses provided by the study participants through Google forms.\n\nraw-results-RQ1/\n\nContains the raw results for RQ1. Specifically, the directory contains a subdirectory for each group (G1-G10). Each subdirectory contains: - For each user (named using their Prolific IDs, a directory containing, for each question (Q1-Q6) the produced python code (Qn.py) its output (QnR.txt) and its StdErr output (QnErr.txt). - \"expected-outputs/\": A directory containing the expected outputs for each task (Qn.txt).\n\nworking-results/RQ1-RQ2-files-for-statistical-analysis/\n\nContains three .csv files used as input for conducting the statistical analysis and drawing the graphs for addressing the first two research questions of the study. Specifically:\n\n\n\n\n\nConstructUsage.csv contains the declared frequency usage of the three functional constructs object of the study. This file is used to draw Figure 4. The file contains an entry for each participant, reporting the (text-coded) frequency of construct usage for Comprehension, Lambda, and MRF.\n\n\n\n\nRQ1.csv contains the collected data used for the mixed-effect logistic regression relating the use of functional constructs with the correctness of the change task, as well as the logistic regression relating the use of map/reduce/filter functions with the correctness of the change task. The csv file contains an entry for each answer provided by each subject, and features the following columns:\n\n\n\nGroup: experimental group to which the participant is assigned\n\nUser: user ID\n\nTime: task time in seconds\n\nApprovals: number of approvals on previous tasks performed on Prolific\n\nStudent: whether the participant declared themselves as a student\n\nSection: section of the questionnaire (lambda, comp, or mrf)\n\nConstruct: specific construct being presented (same as \"Section\" for lambda and comp, for mrf it says whether it is a map, reduce, or filter)\n\nQuestion: question id, from Q1 to Q6, indicate the ordering of the question\n\nMainFactor: main factor treatment for the given question - \"f\" for functional, \"p\" for procedural counterpart\n\nOutcome: TRUE if the task was correctly performed, FALSE otherwise\n\nComplexity: cyclomatic complexity of the construct (empty for mrf)\n\nUsageFrequency: usage frequency of the given construct\n\n\n\n\n\nRQ1Paired-RQ2.csv contains the collected data used for the ordinal logistic regression of the relationship between the perceived ease of understanding of the functional constructs and (i) participants\u0027 usage frequency, and (ii) constructs\u0027 complexity (except for map/reduce/filter). The file features a row for each participant, and the columns are the following:\n\n\n\nGroup: experimental group to which the participant is assigned\n\nUser: user ID\n\nTime: task time in seconds\n\nApprovals: number of approvals on previous tasks performed on Prolific\n\nStudent: whether the participant declared themselves as a student\n\nLambdaF: result for the change task related to a lambda construct\n\nLambdaP: result for the change task related to the procedural counterpart of a lambda construct\n\nCompF: result for the change task related to a comprehension construct\n\nCompP: result for the change task related to the procedural counterpart of a comprehension construct\n\nMrfF: result for the change task related to an MRF construct\n\nMrfP: result for the change task related to the procedural counterpart of a MRF construct\n\nLambdaComp: perceived understandability level for the comparison task (RQ2) between a lambda and its procedural counterpart\n\nCompComp: perceived understandability level for the comparison task (RQ2) between a comprehension and its procedural counterpart\n\nMrfComp: perceived understandability level for the comparison task (RQ2) between a MRF and its procedural counterpart\n\nLambdaCompCplx: cyclomatic complexity of the lambda construct involved in the comparison task (RQ2)\n\nCompCompCplx: cyclomatic complexity of the comprehension construct involved in the comparison task (RQ2)\n\nMrfCompType: type of MRF construct (map, reduce, or filter) used in the comparison task (RQ2)\n\nLambdaUsageFrequency: self-declared usage frequency on lambda constructs\n\nCompUsageFrequency: self-declared usage frequency on comprehension constructs\n\nMrfUsageFrequency: self-declared usage frequency on MRF constructs\n\nLambdaComparisonAssessment: outcome of the manual assessment of the answer to the \"check question\" required for the lambda comparison (\"yes\" means valid, \"no\" means wrong, \"moderatechatgpt\" and \"extremechatgpt\" are the results of GPTZero)\n\nCompComparisonAssessment: as above, but for comprehension\n\nMrfComparisonAssessment: as above, but for MRF\n\n\n\n\nworking-results/inter-rater-RQ3-files/\n\nThis directory contains four .csv files used as input for computing the inter-rater agreement for the manual labeling used for addressing RQ3. Specifically, you will find one file for each functional construct, i.e., comprehension.csv, lambda.csv, and mrf.csv, and a different file used for highlighting the reasons why participants prefer to use the procedural paradigm, i.e., procedural.csv.\n\nworking-results/RQ2ManualValidation.csv\n\nThis file contains the results of the manual validation being done to sanitize the answers provided by our participants used for addressing RQ2. Specifically, we coded the behaviour description using four different levels: (i) correct (\"yes\"), (ii) somewhat correct (\"partial\"), (iii) wrong (\"no\"), and (iv) automatically generated. The file features a row for each participant, and the columns are the following:\n\n\n\nID: ID we used to refer the participant in the paper\u0027s qualitative analysis\n\nGroup: experimental group to which the participant is assigned\n\nProlificID: user ID\n\nComparison for lambda construct description: answer provided by the user for the lambda comparison task\n\nFinal Classification: our assessment of the lambda comparison answer\n\nComparison for comprehension description: answer provided by the user for the comprehension comparison task\n\nFinal Classification: our assessment of the comprehension comparison answer\n\nComparison for MRF description: answer provided by the user for the MRF comparison task\n\nFinal Classification: our assessment of the MRF comparison answer\n\n\nworking-results/RQ3ManualValidation.xlsx\n\nThis file contains the results of the open coding applied to address our third research question. Specifically, you will find four sheets, one for each functional construct and one for the procedural paradigm. Each sheet reports the provided answers together with the categories assigned to them. Each sheet contains the following columns:\n\n\n\nID: ID we used to refer the participant in the paper\u0027s qualitative analysis\n\nGroup: experimental group to which the participant is assigned\n\nProlificID: user ID (as in the tables from the quantitative analysis)\n\n: question asked to the user\n\nFinal Classification: The outcome of our categorization according to the taxonomy shown in Table 10.\n\n\nScripts to reproduce the results and instructions for running them\n\n\u00a0\n\nFuncConstructs-Statistics.r\n\nThis file contains an R script that you can reuse to re-run all the analyses conducted and discussed in the paper.\n\nFuncConstructs-Statistics.ipynb\n\nThis file contains the code to re-execute all the analysis conducted in the paper as a Jupyter Notebook (using the R Kernel).\n\nrun-analysis.sh\n\nThis script can be used to run the R script FuncConstructs-Statistics.r using a Docker container (see Option 1 below) in Unix operating systems.\n\nrun-analysis.bat\n\nThis script can be used to run the R script FuncConstructs-Statistics.r using a Docker container (see Option 1 below) in Windows operating systems (power shell recommended).\n\nrun-jupyter-container.sh\n\nThis script can be used to run a local Jupyter server (with R kernel and all required packages) from a Docker container (see Option 3 below) in Unix operating system.\n\nrun-jupyter-container.bat\n\nThis script can be used to run a local Jupyter server (with R kernel and all required packages) from a Docker container (see Option 3 below) in Windows operating systems (power shell recommended).\n\nHow to Run the scripts\n\nThere are four options to run the scripts. In all cases, one has first to open a shell terminal window (e.g., bash or sh in Unixes) in the replication package directory. For Windows, we suggest to use a Power Shell.\n\n\n\n\n\nRunning the R script using Dockerized R installation: this is the simplest option, and it simply requires a running Docker engine. In Unix (MacOS, Linux), to produce the results, one has to run the shell script \"run-analysis.sh\" (e.g., by typing sh run-analysis.sh or simply ./run-analysis.sh after making it executable). In Windows, one has to run the script \"run-analysis.bat\" instead (by typing .\\run-analysis.bat). This script (either .sh or .bat) will:\n\n\n\nPull a docker image named mdipenta/rexp which contains an R installation with all required packages.\n\n\n\nRun R from the container created from the image and produce the paper\u0027s results under a directory named results/.\n\n\n\n\nNote: An alternative would be to run everything from inside the container, after running it in interactive mode. \u003ca href=\"https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8191782\"\u003ehttps://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8191782\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eLicense\u003c/strong\u003e: \u003ca\u003eGPL V3.0\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis package contains folders and files with code and data used in the study described in the paper. In the following, we first provide all fields required for the submission, and then report a detailed description of all repository folders.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eArtifact Description\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003ePurpose\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe artifact is about a controlled experiment aimed at investigating the extent to which Pythonic functional constructs have an impact on source code understandability. The artifact archive contains:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003col\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eThe material to allow replicating the study (see Section \u003ca\u003eExperimental-Material\u003c/a\u003e)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eRaw quantitative results, working datasets, and scripts to replicate the statistical analyses reported in the paper. Specifically, the executable part of the replication package reproduces figures and tables of the quantitative analysis (RQ1 and RQ2) of the paper starting from the working datasets.\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003eSpreadsheets used for the qualitative analysis (RQ3).\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ol\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eWe apply for the following badges:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eAvailable and reusable\u003c/strong\u003e: because we provide all the material that can be used to replicate the experiment, but also to perform the statistical analyses and the qualitative analyses (spreadsheets, in this case)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eProvenance\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003ePaper preprint link:\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ca href=\"https://mdipenta.github.io/files/ICSE24_funcExperiment.pdf\"\u003ehttps://mdipenta.github.io/files/ICSE24_funcExperiment.pdf\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cstrong\u003eArtifacts:\u003c/strong\u003e \u003ca href=\"https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8191782\"\u003ehttps://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8191782\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eData\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eResults have been obtained by conducting the controlled experiment involving \u003ca href=\"https://www.prolific.com/\"\u003eProlific\u003c/a\u003eworkers as participants. Data collection and processing followed a protocol approved by the University ethical board. Note that all data enclosed in the artifact is completely anonymized and does not contain sensible information.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eFurther details about the provided dataset can be found in the Section \u003ca\u003eResults\u0027 directory and files\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003eSetup and Usage (for executable artifacts):\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eSee the Section \u003ca\u003eScripts to reproduce the results, and instructions for running them\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003e\u003ca\u003eExperiment-Material/\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eContains the material used for the experiment, and, specifically, the following subdirectories:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003e\u003ca\u003eGoogle-Forms/\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eContains (as PDF documents) the questionnaires submitted to the ten experimental groups.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003e\u003ca\u003eTask-Sources/\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eContains, for each experimental group (G-1...G-10), the sources used to produce the Google Forms, and, specifically: - The cover letter (Letter.docx). - A directory for each experimental task (Lambda 1, Lambda 2, Comp 1, Comp 2, MRF 1, MRF 2, Lambda Comparison, Comp Comparison, MRF Comparison). Each directory contains: (i) the exercise text (in both Word and .txt format), the source code snippet, and its .png image to be used in the form. \u003cstrong\u003eNote:\u003c/strong\u003e the \"Comparison\" tasks do not have any exercise as the purpose is always the same, i.e., to compare the (perceived) understandability of the snippets and return the results of the comparison.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003e\u003ca\u003eCode-Examples-Table1/\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eContains the source code snippets used as objects of the study (the same you can find under \"Task-Sources/\"), named as reported in Table 1.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2\u003eResults\u0027 directory and files\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u0026nbsp;\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003e\u003ca\u003eraw-responses/\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eContains, as spreadsheets, the raw responses provided by the study participants through Google forms.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3\u003e\u003ca\u003eraw-results-RQ1/\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eContains the raw results for RQ1. Specifically, the directory contains a subdirectory for each group (G1-G10). Each subdirectory contains: - For each user (named using their Prolific IDs, a directory containing, for each question (Q1-Q6) the produced python code (Qn.py) its output (QnR.txt) and its StdErr output (QnErr.txt). - \"expected-outputs/\": A directory containing the expected outputs for each task (Qn.txt).\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch4\u003e\u003ca\u003eworking-results/RQ1-RQ2-files-for-statistical-analysis/\u003c/a\u003e\u003c/h4\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eContains three .csv files used as input for conducting the statistical analysis and drawing the graphs for addressing the first two research questions of the study. Specifically:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca\u003eConstructUsage.csv\u003c/a\u003e contains the declared frequency usage of the three functional constructs object of the study. This file is used to draw Figure 4. The file contains an entry for each participant, reporting the (text-coded) frequency of construct usage for Comprehension, Lambda, and MRF.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca\u003eRQ1.csv\u003c/a\u003e contains the collected data used for the mixed-effect logistic regression relating the use of functional constructs with the correctness of the change task, as well as the logistic regression relating the use of map/reduce/filter functions with the correctness of the change task. The csv file contains an entry for each answer provided by each subject, and features the following columns:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eGroup\u003c/em\u003e: experimental group to which the participant is assigned\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eUser\u003c/em\u003e: user ID\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eTime\u003c/em\u003e: task time in seconds\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eApprovals\u003c/em\u003e: number of approvals on previous tasks performed on Prolific\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eStudent\u003c/em\u003e: whether the participant declared themselves as a student\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eSection\u003c/em\u003e: section of the questionnaire (lambda, comp, or mrf)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eConstruct\u003c/em\u003e: specific construct being presented (same as \"Section\" for lambda and comp, for mrf it says whether it is a map, reduce, or filter)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eQuestion\u003c/em\u003e: question id, from Q1 to Q6, indicate the ordering of the question\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eMainFactor\u003c/em\u003e: main factor treatment for the given question - \"f\" for functional, \"p\" for procedural counterpart\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eOutcome\u003c/em\u003e: TRUE if the task was correctly performed, FALSE otherwise\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eComplexity\u003c/em\u003e: cyclomatic complexity of the construct (empty for mrf)\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eUsageFrequency\u003c/em\u003e: usage frequency of the given construct\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003c/ul\u003e\n\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\n\u003cp\u003e\u003ca\u003eRQ1Paired-RQ2.csv\u003c/a\u003e contains the collected data used for the ordinal logistic regression of the relationship between the perceived ease of understanding of the functional constructs and (i) participants\u0027 usage frequency, and (ii) constructs\u0027 complexity (except for map/reduce/filter). The file features a row for each participant, and the columns are the following:\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cul\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eGroup\u003c/em\u003e: experimental group to which the participant is assigned\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eUser\u003c/em\u003e: user ID\u003c/li\u003e\n\u003cli\u003e\u003cem\u003eTime\u003c/em\u003e: task time in In the following, we first provide all fields required for the submission, and then report a detailed description of all repository folders.\n\nArtifact Description\n\nPurpose\n\nThe artifact is about a controlled experiment aimed at investigating the extent to which Pythonic functional constructs have an impact on source code understandability. The artifact archive contains:\n\n\n\nThe material to allow replicating the study (see Section Experimental-Material)\n\nRaw quantitative results, working datasets, and scripts to replicate the statistical analyses reported in the paper. Specifically, the executable part of the replication package reproduces figures and tables of the quantitative analysis (RQ1 and RQ2) of the paper starting from the working datasets.\n\nSpreadsheets used for the qualitative analysis (RQ3).\n\n\nWe apply for the following badges:\n\n\n\nAvailable and reusable: because we provide all the material that can be used to replicate the experiment, but also to perform the statistical analyses and the qualitative analyses (spreadsheets, in this case)\n\n\nProvenance\n\n\n\nPaper preprint link: https://mdipenta.github.io/files/ICSE24_funcExperiment.pdf\n\nArtifacts: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8191782\n\n\nData\n\nResults have been obtained by conducting the controlled experiment involving Prolificworkers as participants. Data collection and processing followed a protocol approved by the University ethical board. Note that all data enclosed in the artifact is completely anonymized and does not contain sensible information.\n\nFurther details about the provided dataset can be found in the Section Results\u0027 directory and files\n\nSetup and Usage (for executable artifacts):\n\nSee the Section Scripts to reproduce the results, and instructions for running them\n\nExperiment-Material/\n\nContains the material used for the experiment, and, specifically, the following subdirectories:\n\nGoogle-Forms/\n\nContains (as PDF documents) the questionnaires submitted to the ten experimental groups.\n\nTask-Sources/\n\nContains, for each experimental group (G-1...G-10), the sources used to produce the Google Forms, and, specifically: - The cover letter (Letter.docx). - A directory for each experimental task (Lambda 1, Lambda 2, Comp 1, Comp 2, MRF 1, MRF 2, Lambda Comparison, Comp Comparison, MRF Comparison). Each directory contains: (i) the exercise text (in both Word and .txt format), the source code snippet, and its .png image to be used in the form. Note: the \"Comparison\" tasks do not have any exercise as the purpose is always the same, i.e., to compare the (perceived) understandability of the snippets and return the results of the comparison.\n\nCode-Examples-Table1/\n\nContains the source code snippets used as objects of the study (the same you can find under \"Task-Sources/\"), named as reported in Table 1.\n\nResults\u0027 directory and files\n\n\u00a0\n\nraw-responses/\n\nContains, as spreadsheets, the raw responses provided by the study participants through Google forms.\n\nraw-results-RQ1/\n\nContains the raw results for RQ1. Specifically, the directory contains a subdirectory for each group (G1-G10). Each subdirectory contains: - For each user (named using their Prolific IDs, a directory containing, for each question (Q1-Q6) the produced python code (Qn.py) its output (QnR.txt) and its StdErr output (QnErr.txt). - \"expected-outputs/\": A directory containing the expected outputs for each task (Qn.txt).\n\nworking-results/RQ1-RQ2-files-for-statistical-analysis/\n\nContains three .csv files used as input for conducting the statistical analysis and drawing the graphs for addressing the first two research questions of the study. Specifically:\n\n\n\n\n\nConstructUsage.csv contains the declared frequency usage of the three functional constructs object of the study. This file is used to draw Figure 4. The file contains an entry for each participant, reporting the (text-coded) frequency of construct usage for Comprehension, Lambda, and MRF.\n\n\n\n\nRQ1.csv contains the collected data used for the mixed-effect logistic regression relating the use of functional constructs with the correctness of the change task, as well as the logistic regression relating the use of map/reduce/filter functions with the correctness of the change task. The csv file contains an entry for each answer provided by each subject, and features the following columns:\n\n\n\nGroup: experimental group to which the participant is assigned\n\nUser: user ID\n\nTime: task time in seconds\n\nApprovals: number of approvals on previous tasks performed on Prolific\n\nStudent: whether the participant declared themselves as a student\n\nSection: section of the questionnaire (lambda, comp, or mrf)\n\nConstruct: specific construct being presented (same as \"Section\" for lambda and comp, for mrf it says whether it is a map, reduce, or filter)\n\nQuestion: question id, from Q1 to Q6, indicate the ordering of the question\n\nMainFactor: main factor treatment for the given question - \"f\" for functional, \"p\" for procedural counterpart\n\nOutcome: TRUE if the task was correctly performed, FALSE otherwise\n\nComplexity: cyclomatic complexity of the construct (empty for mrf)\n\nUsageFrequency: usage frequency of the given construct\n\n\n\n\n\nRQ1Paired-RQ2.csv contains the collected data used for the ordinal logistic regression of the relationship between the perceived ease of understanding of the functional constructs and (i) participants\u0027 usage frequency, and (ii) constructs\u0027 complexity (except for map/reduce/filter). The file features a row for each participant, and the columns are the following:\n\n\n\nGroup: experimental group to which the participant is assigned\n\nUser: user ID\n\nTime: task time in seconds\n\nApprovals: number of approvals on previous tasks performed on Prolific\n\nStudent: whether the participant declared themselves as a student\n\nLambdaF: result for the change task related to a lambda construct\n\nLambdaP: result for the change task related to the procedural counterpart of a lambda construct\n\nCompF: result for the change task related to a comprehension construct\n\nCompP: result for the change task related to the procedural counterpart of a comprehension construct\n\nMrfF: result for the change task related to an MRF construct\n\nMrfP: result for the change task related to the procedural counterpart of a MRF construct\n\nLambdaComp: perceived understandability level for the comparison task (RQ2) between a lambda and its procedural counterpart\n\nCompComp: perceived understandability level for the comparison task (RQ2) between a comprehension and its procedural counterpart\n\nMrfComp: perceived understandability level for the complexity of the comprehension construct involved in the comparison task (RQ2)\n\nMrfCompType: type of MRF construct (map, reduce, or filter) used in the comparison task MRF\n\n\n\n\nworking-results/inter-rater-RQ3-files/\n\nThis directory contains four .csv files used as input for computing the inter-rater agreement for the manual labeling used for addressing RQ3. In Windows, one has to run the script \"run-analysis.bat\" instead (by typing .\\run-analysis.bat). This script (either .sh or .bat) will:\n\n\n\nPull a docker image named mdipenta/rexp which contains an R installation with all required packages.\n\n\n\nRun R from the container created from the image and produce the paper\u0027s results under a directory named results/.\n\n\n\n\nNote: An alternative would be to run everything from inside the container, after running it in interactive mode. To this aim, please execute the following commands:\n\n\n\nIn Unix: docker run -v${PWD}:/data --rm -ti --name shell mdipenta/rexp:latest bashin Windows: docker run -v %cd%:/data --rm -ti --name shell mdipenta/rexp:latest bash\n\ncd data\n\nR --no-save \u003c FuncConstructs-Statistics.r After exiting the container, the \"results\" directory will be again populated with the study results.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\nRunning the R script from own R installation: this option works if one has an R installation already (or wants to use an R installation) without relying on the Docker image. The steps to be followed are:\n\n\n\nUncomment the install.packages(..) instruction in the first lines of the script. This will allow for the installation of the required packages.\n\nJust run, from the current directory, the script FuncConstructs-Statistics.r, using the command Rscript FuncConstructs-Statistics.r (making sure the directory containing Rscript is in your PATH, this should work fine in Unixes, it might require to modify the PATH environment variable in Windows). Should you experience problems with the first part of the script (installations), try to execute the install.packages(..) statement from your R GUI, and then run the script again.\n\n\n\n\n\nUsing the Jupyter Notebook using a Dockerized Jupyter lab with R kernel: this option allows for opening the Jupyter Notebook with all results without having to install Jupyter with the R kernel, nor all the required R packages. The steps required are:\n\n\n\nRun the ./run-jupyter-container.sh (Unix) or .\\run-jupyter-container.bat (Windows). It will download the mdipenta/myjupyter image and run Jupyter lab from it.\n\nOpen a browser on localhost:8888 (or if it does not work, 127.0.0.1:8888) and, when being asked for a password, type docker.\n\nFrom the Jupyter lab page, open the \"FuncConstruct-Statistics.ipynb\" notebook, and (if you wish) re-run it, or simply browse its results. Note: differently from options 1 and 2, results are not saved, but just displayed in the notebook.\n\n\n\n\n\nUsing the Jupyter Notebook from your installation: this is similar to Option 3, but it can work if you have already Jupyter lab installed, with the R kernel enabled (for details see: https://github.com/IRkernel/IRkernel). In the following, we first provide all fields required for the submission, and then report a detailed description of all repository folders. ## Artifact Description ### Purpose The artifact is about a controlled experiment aimed at investigating the extent to which Pythonic functional constructs have an impact on source code understandability. The artifact archive contains: 1. The material to allow replicating the study (see Section [Experimental-Material](#material)) 2. Raw quantitative results, working datasets, and scripts to replicate the statistical analyses reported in the paper. Specifically, the executable part of the replication package reproduces figures and tables of the quantitative analysis (RQ1 and RQ2) of the paper starting from the working datasets. 3. Spreadsheets used for the qualitative analysis (RQ3). We apply for the following badges: - **Available and reusable**: because we provide all the material that can be used to replicate the experiment, but also to perform the statistical analyses and the qualitative analyses (spreadsheets, in this case) ### Provenance - **Paper preprint link:** [https://mdipenta.github.io/files/ICSE24_funcExperiment.pdf](https://mdipenta.github.io/files/ICSE24_funcExperiment.pdf) - **Artifacts:** [https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8191782](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.8191782) ### Data Results have been obtained by conducting the controlled experiment involving [Prolific](https://www.prolific.com) workers as participants. Data collection and processing followed a protocol approved by the University ethical board. Note that all data enclosed in the artifact is completely anonymized and does not contain sensible information. Further details about the provided dataset can be found in the Section [Results' directory and files](#results) ### Setup and Usage (for executable artifacts): See the Section [Scripts to reproduce the results, and instructions for running them](#scripts) ## [Experiment-Material/](Experiment-Material/) Contains the material used for the experiment, and, specifically, the following subdirectories: ### [Google-Forms/](Experiment-Material/Google-Forms/) Contains (as PDF documents) the questionnaires submitted to the ten experimental groups. ### [Task-Sources/](Experiment-Material/Task-Sources/) Contains, for each experimental group (G-1...G-10), the sources used to produce the Google Forms, and, specifically: - The cover letter (Letter.docx). - A directory for each experimental task (Lambda 1, Lambda 2, Comp 1, Comp 2, MRF 1, MRF 2, Lambda Comparison, Comp Comparison, MRF Comparison). Each directory contains: (i) the exercise text (in both Word and .txt format), the source code snippet, and its .png image to be used in the form. **Note:** the "Comparison" tasks do not have any exercise as the purpose is always the same, i.e., to compare the (perceived) understandability of the snippets and return the results of the comparison. ### [Code-Examples-Table1/](Experiment-Material/Code-Examples-Table1/) Contains the source code snippets used as objects of the study (the same you can find under "Task-Sources/"), named as reported in Table 1. ## Results' directory and files ### [raw-responses/](raw-responses/) Contains, as spreadsheets, the raw responses provided by the study participants through Google forms. ### [raw-results-RQ1/](raw-results-RQ1/) Contains the raw results for RQ1. Specifically, the directory contains a subdirectory for each group (G1-G10). Each subdirectory contains: - For each user (named using their Prolific IDs, a directory containing, for each question (Q1-Q6) the produced python code (Qn.py) its output (QnR.txt) and its StdErr output (QnErr.txt). - "expected-outputs/": A directory containing the expected outputs for each task (Qn.txt). #### [working-results/RQ1-RQ2-files-for-statistical-analysis/](working-results/RQ1-RQ2-files-for-statistical-analysis/) Contains three .csv files used as input for conducting the statistical analysis and drawing the graphs for addressing the first two research questions of the study. Specifically: - [ConstructUsage.csv](working-results/RQ1-RQ2-files-for-statistical-analysis/ConstructUsage.csv) contains the declared frequency usage of the three functional constructs object of the study. This file is used to draw Figure 4. The file contains an entry for each participant, reporting the (text-coded) frequency of construct usage for Comprehension, Lambda, and MRF. - [RQ1.csv](working-results/RQ1-RQ2-files-for-statistical-analysis/RQ1.csv) contains the collected data used for the mixed-effect logistic regression relating the use of functional constructs with the correctness of the change task, as well as the logistic regression relating the use of map/reduce/filter functions with the correctness of the change task. The csv file contains an entry for each answer provided by each subject, and features the following columns: - *Group*: experimental group to which the participant is assigned - *User*: user ID - *Time*: task time in seconds - *Approvals*: number of approvals on previous tasks performed on Prolific - *Student*: whether the participant declared themselves as a student - *Section*: section of the questionnaire (lambda, comp, or mrf) - *Construct*: specific construct being presented (same as "Section" for lambda and comp, for mrf it says whether it is a map, reduce, or filter) - *Question*: question id, from Q1 to Q6, indicate the ordering of the question - *MainFactor*: main factor treatment for the given question - "f" for functional, "p" for procedural counterpart - *Outcome*: TRUE if the task was correctly performed, FALSE otherwise - *Complexity*: cyclomatic complexity of the construct (empty for mrf) - *UsageFrequency*: usage frequency of the given construct - [RQ1Paired-RQ2.csv](working-results/RQ1-RQ2-files-for-statistical-analysis/RQ1Paired-RQ2.csv) contains the collected data used for the ordinal logistic regression of the relationship between the perceived ease of understanding of the functional constructs and (i) participants' usage frequency, and (ii) constructs' complexity (except for map/reduce/filter). The file features a row for each participant, and the columns are the following: - *Group*: experimental group to which the participant is assigned - *User*: user ID - *Time*: task time in seconds - *Approvals*: number of approvals on previous tasks performed on Prolific - *Student*: whether the participant declared themselves as a student - *LambdaF*: result for the change task related to a lambda construct - *LambdaP*: result for the change task related to the procedural counterpart of a lambda construct - *CompF*: result for the change task related to a comprehension construct - *CompP*: result for the change task related to the procedural counterpart of a comprehension construct - *MrfF*: result for the change task related to an MRF construct - *MrfP*: result for the change task related to the procedural counterpart of a MRF construct - *LambdaComp*: perceived understandability level for the comparison task (RQ2) between a lambda and its procedural counterpart - *CompComp*: perceived understandability level for the comparison task (RQ2) between a comprehension and its procedural counterpart - *MrfComp*: perceived understandability level for the comparison task (RQ2) between a MRF and its procedural counterpart - *LambdaCompCplx*: cyclomatic complexity of the lambda construct involved in the comparison task (RQ2) - *CompCompCplx*: cyclomatic complexity of the comprehension construct involved in the comparison task (RQ2) - *MrfCompType*: type of MRF construct (map, reduce, or filter) used in the comparison task (RQ2) - *LambdaUsageFrequency*: self-declared usage frequency on lambda constructs - *CompUsageFrequency*: self-declared usage frequency on comprehension constructs - *MrfUsageFrequency*: self-declared usage frequency on MRF constructs - *LambdaComparisonAssessment*: outcome of the manual assessment of the answer to the "check question" required for the lambda comparison ("yes" means valid, "no" means wrong, "moderate_chatgpt" and "extreme_chatgpt" are the results of GPTZero) - *CompComparisonAssessment*: as above, but for comprehension - *MrfComparisonAssessment*: as above, but for MRF ### [working-results/inter-rater-RQ3-files/](working-results/inter-rater-RQ3-files/) This directory contains four .csv files used as input for computing the inter-rater agreement for the manual labeling used for addressing RQ3. Specifically, you will find one file for each functional construct, i.e., comprehension.csv, lambda.csv, and mrf.csv, and a different file used for highlighting the reasons why participants prefer to use the procedural paradigm, i.e., procedural.csv. ### [working-results/RQ2ManualValidation.csv](working-results/RQ2ManualValidation.csv) This file contains the results of the manual validation being done to sanitize the answers provided by our participants used for addressing RQ2. Specifically, we coded the behaviour description using four different levels: (i) correct ("yes"), (ii) somewhat correct ("partial"), (iii) wrong ("no"), and (iv) automatically generated. The file features a row for each participant, and the columns are the following: - *ID*: ID we used to refer the participant in the paper's qualitative analysis - *Group*: experimental group to which the participant is assigned - *ProlificID*: user ID - *Comparison for lambda construct description*: answer provided by the user for the lambda comparison task - *Final Classification*: our assessment of the lambda comparison answer - *Comparison for comprehension description*: answer provided by the user for the comprehension comparison task - *Final Classification*: our assessment of the comprehension comparison answer - *Comparison for MRF description*: answer provided by the user for the MRF comparison task - *Final Classification*: our assessment of the MRF comparison answer ### [working-results/RQ3ManualValidation.xlsx](working-results/RQ3ManualValidation.xlsx) This file contains the results of the open coding applied to address our third research question. Specifically, you will find four sheets, one for each functional construct and one for the procedural paradigm. Each sheet reports the provided answers together with the categories assigned to them. Each sheet contains the following columns: - *ID*: ID we used to refer the participant in the paper's qualitative analysis - *Group*: experimental group to which the participant is assigned - *ProlificID*: user ID (as in the tables from the quantitative analysis) - **: question asked to the user - *Final Classification*: The outcome of our categorization according to the taxonomy shown in Table 10. ## Scripts to reproduce the results and instructions for running them ### [FuncConstructs-Statistics.r](FuncConstructs-Statistics.r) This file contains an R script that you can reuse to re-run all the analyses conducted and discussed in the paper. ### [FuncConstructs-Statistics.ipynb](FuncConstructs-Statistics.ipynb) This file contains the code to re-execute all the analysis conducted in the paper as a Jupyter Notebook (using the R Kernel). ### [run-analysis.sh](run-analysis.sh) This script can be used to run the R script `FuncConstructs-Statistics.r` using a Docker container (see Option 1 below) in Unix operating systems. ### [run-analysis.bat](run-analysis.bat) This script can be used to run the R script `FuncConstructs-Statistics.r` using a Docker container (see Option 1 below) in Windows operating systems (power shell recommended). ### [run-jupyter-container.sh](run-jupyter-container.sh) This script can be used to run a local Jupyter server (with R kernel and all required packages) from a Docker container (see Option 3 below) in Unix operating system. ### [run-jupyter-container.bat](run-jupyter-container.bat) This script can be used to run a local Jupyter server (with R kernel and all required packages) from a Docker container (see Option 3 below) in Windows operating systems (power shell recommended). ### How to Run the scripts There are four options to run the scripts. In all cases, one has first to open a shell terminal window (e.g., bash or sh in Unixes) in the replication package directory. For Windows, we suggest to use a Power Shell. 1. **Running the R script using Dockerized R installation**: this is the simplest option, and it simply requires a running Docker engine. In **Unix (MacOS, Linux)**, to produce the results, one has to run the shell script "run-analysis.sh" (e.g., by typing `sh run-analysis.sh` or simply `./run-analysis.sh` after making it executable). In **Windows**, one has to run the script "run-analysis.bat" instead (by typing `.\run-analysis.bat`). This script (either .sh or .bat) will: - Pull a docker image named `mdipenta/rexp` which contains an R installation with all required packages. - Run R from the container created from the image and produce the paper's results under a directory named `results/`. - **Note:** An alternative would be to run everything from inside the container, after running it in interactive mode. To this aim, please execute the following commands: 1. In **Unix**: `docker run -v${PWD}:/data --rm -ti --name shell mdipenta/rexp:latest bash` in **Windows**: `docker run -v %cd%:/data --rm -ti --name shell mdipenta/rexp:latest bash` 2. `cd data` 3. `R --no-save < FuncConstructs-Statistics.r` After exiting the container, the "results" directory will be again populated with the study results. 2. **Running the R script from own R installation**: this option works if one has an R installation already (or wants to use an R installation) without relying on the Docker image. The steps to be followed are: - Uncomment the `install.packages(..)` instruction in the first lines of the script. This will allow for the installation of the required packages. - Just run, from the current directory, the script `FuncConstructs-Statistics.r`, using the command `Rscript FuncConstructs-Statistics.r` (making sure the directory containing Rscript is in your PATH, this should work fine in Unixes, it might require to modify the PATH environment variable in Windows). Should you experience problems with the first part of the script (installations), try to execute the `install.packages(..)` statement from your R GUI, and then run the script again. 3. **Using the Jupyter Notebook using a Dockerized Jupyter lab with R kernel**: this option allows for opening the Jupyter Notebook with all results without having to install Jupyter with the R kernel, nor all the required R packages. The steps required are: - Run the `./run-jupyter-container.sh` (**Unix**) or `.\run-jupyter-container.bat` (**Windows**). It will download the `mdipenta/myjupyter` image and run Jupyter lab from it. - Open a browser on [localhost:8888](http://localhost:8888) (or if it does not work, [127.0.0.1:8888)](http://127.0.0.1:8888) and, when being asked for a password, type `docker`. - From the Jupyter lab page, open the "FuncConstruct-Statistics.ipynb" notebook, and (if you wish) re-run it, or simply browse its results. Note: differently from options 1 and 2, results are not saved, but just displayed in the notebook. 4. **Using the Jupyter Notebook from your installation**: this is similar to Option 3, but it can work if you have already Jupyter lab installed, with the R kernel enabled (for details see: [https://github.com/IRkernel/IRkernel](https://github.com/IRkernel/IRkernel)). The steps to follow are: - Run jupyter lab (e.g., jupyter lab from the command line) and open it on a webpage. - Open the `FuncConstruct-Statistics.ipynb` notebook. - If you want to re-execute it, uncomment the `install.packages()` line. [?2004h

[?2004l# Uncomment the following line to run this script from own R installation
#install.packages(c("likert", "parameters", "reshape", "lme4","xtable","exact2x2","MASS","irr"))

library(likert)
library(parameters)
library(reshape)
library(lme4)
library(xtable)
library(exact2x2)
library(MASS)
library(irr)


inputDir="working-results//RQ1-RQ2-files-for-statistical-analysis"
outputDir="results"
irrDir="working-results//inter-rater-RQ3-files"

# Creates the output directory
dir.create(outputDir)

# Writes a data frame into a CSV file
toCSV<-function(data,fileName){
    outFile=paste(outputDir,fileName,sep="//")
    write.csv(data,file=outFile,quote=FALSE,row.names=FALSE)
}

# Writes a data object into a textual file
toTxt<-function(data,fileName){
    outFile=paste(outputDir,fileName,sep="//")
    capture.output(
        print(data),
        file=outFile)
}

# Writes a data frame into a LaTex file, creating a table with a label and caption
toLaTex<-function(data,fileName,label,caption){
    outFileLatex=paste(outputDir,fileName,sep="//")
    capture.output(
        print(xtable(data,digits=3,label=label,caption=caption)),
        file=outFileLatex)
}

##############################
# DEMOGRAPHICS
##############################

### Likert Plot of constructs' usage (Figure 4)

t2<-read.csv(paste(inputDir,"ConstructUsage.csv",sep="//"))
t2<-subset(t2,t2$Comprehension!="Never" | t2$Lambda!="Never" | t2$MRF!="Never")
mylevels <- c('Never', 'Less than 25%', 'Between 25% and 75%', 'More than 75%')
s2 <- as.data.frame(lapply(t2,function(x) {factor(x,levels=mylevels)}))


l=likert(s2)
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0)) 
pdf(file=paste(outputDir,"Figure-4-ConstructUsage.pdf",sep="//"),width=10,height=3)
p<-plot(l,text.size=4,group.order=c("Lambda","Comprehension","MRF"))
p+theme(axis.title.x=element_text(size = 16),
        axis.text.x=element_text(size = 14),
        axis.text.y=element_text(size = 14),
        text=element_text(size = 14),
        legend.title=element_text(size = 14),
        legend.text=element_text(size = 14))
dev.off()

##########################################
# RQ1 - Descriptive statistics (Table 2)
##########################################
t<-read.csv(paste(inputDir,"RQ1.csv",sep="//"))
sections<-c("lambda","comp","mrf")
res<-list(Construct=c(),Ftrue=c(),Ffalse=c(),Fperc=c(),Ptrue=c(),Pfalse=c(),Pperc=c())
for(section in sections)
{
  tsub<-subset(t,t$Section==section)
  tt<-table(tsub$Outcome,tsub$MainFactor)
  res$Construct=c(res$Construct,section)
  
  res$Ftrue=c(res$Ftrue,tt[2,1])
  res$Ffalse=c(res$Ffalse,tt[1,1])
  res$Fperc=c(res$Fperc,100*tt[2,1]/(tt[1,1]+tt[2,1]))
  
  res$Ptrue=c(res$Ptrue,tt[2,2])
  res$Pfalse=c(res$Pfalse,tt[1,2])
  res$Pperc=c(res$Pperc,100*tt[2,2]/(tt[1,2]+tt[2,2]))
}
res=data.frame(res)
res

outFile=paste(outputDir,"Table-2-descriptive.csv",sep="//")
toCSV(res,"Table-2-descriptive.csv")
toLaTex(res,"Table-2-descriptive.tex","tab:descr","Number and percentage of correct/wrong tasks for functional constructs and their procedural alternatives")




############################################################
# RQ1 - Generalized linear models for different constructs
############################################################


# Add 1 offset to Complexity as in the files it starts from 0
t$Complexity=t$Complexity+1

print("LAMBDA:")
tLambda<-subset(t,t$Section=="lambda" & t$UsageFrequency>1)
tLambda=droplevels(tLambda)
attach(tLambda)

model<-glmer(Outcome~MainFactor*Complexity+UsageFrequency+Approvals+Student+(1|User),family="binomial",data=tLambda,control=glmerControl(optimizer="nloptwrap",calc.derivs=FALSE,optCtrl=list(maxfun=2e6)))
smod=summary(model)
smod$coefficients[,4]=p.adjust(smod$coefficients[,4],method="BH")
mc=smod$coefficients
OR=exp(mc[,1])
coeffTable<-cbind(OR,mc)
#pvalues=coeffTable[,5]
#padjusted=p.adjust(pvalues,method="BH")
#coeffTable[,5]=padjusted
toTxt(smod,"Table-3-RQ1-lambda.txt")
toCSV(coeffTable,"Table-3-RQ1-lambda-coeff.txt")
toLaTex(coeffTable,"Table-3-RQ1-lambda-coeff.tex","tab:rq1lambda","RQ$_1$: Mixed-effect logistic regression relating the use of lambdas with the correctness of the change task")


print("COMPREHENSION:")
tComp=subset(t,t$Section=="comp" & t$UsageFrequency>1)
tComp=droplevels(tComp)
attach(tComp)
model<-glmer(Outcome~MainFactor*Complexity+UsageFrequency+Approvals+Student+(1|User),data=tComp,family="binomial",control=glmerControl(optimizer="nloptwrap",calc.derivs=FALSE,optCtrl=list(maxfun=2e6)))
smod=summary(model)
smod$coefficients[,4]=p.adjust(smod$coefficients[,4],method="BH")
mc=smod$coefficients
OR=exp(mc[,1])
coeffTable<-cbind(OR,mc)
#pvalues=coeffTable[,5]
#padjusted=p.adjust(pvalues,method="BH")
#coeffTable[,5]=padjusted
toTxt(smod,"Table-4-RQ1-comp.txt")
toCSV(coeffTable,"Table-4-RQ1-comp-coeff.txt")
toLaTex(coeffTable,"Table-4-RQ1-comp-coeff.tex","tab:rq1comp","RQ$_1$: Mixed-effect logistic regression relating the use of comprehensions with the correctness of the change task")



print("MRF:")
tMrf=subset(t,t$Section=="mrf" & t$UsageFrequency>1)
tMrf=droplevels(tMrf)
attach(tMrf)
model<-glmer(Outcome~MainFactor+UsageFrequency+Approvals+Student+(1|User),data=tMrf,family="binomial",control=glmerControl(optimizer="nloptwrap",calc.derivs=FALSE,optCtrl=list(maxfun=2e6)))
smod=summary(model)
mc=smod$coefficients
smod$coefficients[,4]=p.adjust(smod$coefficients[,4],method="BH")
OR=exp(mc[,1])
coeffTable<-cbind(OR,mc)
#pvalues=coeffTable[,5]
#padjusted=p.adjust(pvalues,method="BH")
#coeffTable[,5]=padjusted
toTxt(smod,"Table-5-RQ1-mrf.txt")
toCSV(coeffTable,"Table-5-RQ1-mrf-coeff.txt")
toLaTex(coeffTable,"Table-5-RQ1-mrf-coeff.tex","tab:rq1mrf","RQ$_1$: Mixed-effect logistic regression relating the use of MRF with the correctness of the change task")


print("MAP:")
tMrf=subset(t,t$Section=="mrf" & t$Construct=="map" & t$UsageFrequency>1)
tMrf=droplevels(tMrf)
attach(tMrf)
model<-glm(Outcome~MainFactor+UsageFrequency+Approvals+Student,data=tMrf,family="binomial")
smod=summary(model)
mc=smod$coefficients
pvalues=mc[,4]
padjusted=p.adjust(pvalues,method="BH")
mc[,4]=padjusted
toCSV(mc,"Table-6-RQ1-map.csv")
caption=paste("RQ$_1$: Logistic regression relating the use of map with the correctness of the change task (AIC=",round(model$aic),")",sep="")
toLaTex(mc,"Table-6-RQ1-map.tex","tab:rq1map",caption)


print("REDUCE:")
tMrf=subset(t,t$Section=="mrf" & t$Construct=="reduce" & t$UsageFrequency>1)
tMrf=droplevels(tMrf)
attach(tMrf)
model<-glm(Outcome~MainFactor+UsageFrequency+Approvals+Student,family="binomial")
smod=summary(model)
mc=smod$coefficients
pvalues=mc[,4]
padjusted=p.adjust(pvalues,method="BH")
mc[,4]=padjusted
toCSV(mc,"Table-7-RQ1-reduce.csv")
caption=paste("RQ$_1$: Logistic regression relating the use of reduce with the correctness of the change task (AIC=",round(model$aic),")",sep="")
toLaTex(mc,"Table-7-RQ1-reduce.tex","tab:rq1reduce",caption)



print("FILTER:")
tMrf=subset(t,t$Section=="mrf" & t$Construct=="filter" & t$UsageFrequency>1)
tMrf=droplevels(tMrf)
attach(tMrf)
model<-glm(Outcome~MainFactor+UsageFrequency+Approvals+Student,family="binomial")
smod=summary(model)
mc=smod$coefficients
pvalues=mc[,4]
padjusted=p.adjust(pvalues,method="BH")
mc[,4]=padjusted
toCSV(mc,"Table-8-RQ1-filter.csv")
caption=paste("RQ$_1$: Logistic regression relating the use of filter with the correctness of the change task (AIC=",round(model$aic),")",sep="")
toLaTex(mc,"Table-8-RQ1-filter.tex","tab:rq1filter",caption)



##############################
# RQ2
##############################

# Reads the dataset
cmp<-read.csv(paste(inputDir,"RQ1Paired-RQ2.csv",sep="//"))

# Prepares the dataset
clambda=subset(cmp,cmp$LambdaUsageFrequency>1 & cmp$LambdaComparisonAssessment!="extreme_chatgpt" & cmp$LambdaComparisonAssessment!="no",select=c(LambdaComp))
clambda[,1]=as.factor(clambda[,1])
ccomp=subset(cmp,cmp$CompUsageFrequency>1 & cmp$CompComparisonAssessment!="extreme_chatgpt" & cmp$CompComparisonAssessment!="no",select=c(CompComp))

ccomp[,1]=as.factor(ccomp[,1])
cmrf=subset(cmp,cmp$MrfUsageFrequency>1 & cmp$MrfComparisonAssessment!="extreme_chatgpt" & cmp$MrfComparisonAssessment!="no",select=c(MrfComp))
cmrf[,1]=as.factor(cmrf[,1])
cmap=subset(cmp,cmp$MrfUsageFrequency>1 & cmp$MrfCompType=="map" & cmp$MrfComparisonAssessment!="extreme_chatgpt" & cmp$MrfComparisonAssessment!="no",select=c(MrfComp))
cmap[,1]=as.factor(cmap[,1])
creduce=subset(cmp,cmp$MrfUsageFrequency>1 & cmp$MrfCompType=="reduce" & cmp$MrfComparisonAssessment!="extreme_chatgpt" & cmp$MrfComparisonAssessment!="no",select=c(MrfComp))
creduce[,1]=as.factor(creduce[,1])
cfilter=subset(cmp,cmp$MrfUsageFrequency>1 & cmp$MrfCompType=="filter" & cmp$MrfComparisonAssessment!="extreme_chatgpt" & cmp$MrfComparisonAssessment!="no",select=c(MrfComp))
cfilter[,1]=as.factor(cfilter[,1])

lenmax=max(c(nrow(clambda),nrow(ccomp),nrow(cmrf)))
col_lambda=c(clambda[,1],rep(NA,lenmax-nrow(clambda)))
col_comp=c(ccomp[,1],rep(NA,lenmax-nrow(ccomp)))
col_mrf=c(cmrf[,1],rep(NA,lenmax-nrow(cmrf)))
col_map=c(cmap[,1],rep(NA,lenmax-nrow(cmap)))
col_reduce=c(creduce[,1],rep(NA,lenmax-nrow(creduce)))
col_filter=c(cfilter[,1],rep(NA,lenmax-nrow(cfilter)))

newdf=data.frame(Lambda=as.factor(col_lambda),Comprehension=as.factor(col_comp),

# Section 1: Expected table
cat > /workspace/expected.md <<'EOTABLE'
**Table 3: RQ1: Mixed-effect logistic regression relating the use of lambdas with the correctness of the change task**

|                  |        |
| ---------------- | ------ |

| **BIC**          | 468.5  |
| **logLik**       | -211.2 |

| Term | OR | Estimate | Std.Error | z value | Pr(>|z|) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

| MainFactorProc | 0.11 | -2.19 | 0.67 | -3.29 | <0.01 |
| Compl. | 0.75 | -0.29 | 0.19 | -1.55 | 0.24 |
| Usage Freq. | 1.32 | 0.28 | 0.23 | 1.20 | 0.24 |
| Approvals | 1.00 | -0.00 | 0.00 | -1.41 | 0.24 |
| StudentTrue | 0.35 | -1.04 | 0.88 | -1.18 | 0.24 |
| MainFactorProc:Compl. | 2.67 | 0.98 | 0.28 | 3.56 | <0.01 |

EOTABLE

# Section 2: Artifact download
mkdir -p /workspace/artifact_tmp
curl -sSfL -o /workspace/artifact_tmp/artifact.zip "https://zenodo.org/api/records/10554377/files/ICSE2024-funcConstructs-Artifacts.zip/content"

# Section 3: Reproduction commands
set -e
cd /workspace/artifact_tmp
unzip -q artifact.zip -d ./artifact
cd artifact/ICSE2024-funcConstructs-Artifacts

# Install system R and core packages (may require root privileges)
# Note: on systems without apt you can skip this and use Docker or an existing R installation.
if command -v apt-get >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  apt-get update || true
  apt-get install -y r-base r-cran-lme4 r-cran-xtable r-cran-reshape r-cran-mass r-cran-nloptr || true
fi

# Install missing CRAN packages if not already present
Rscript -e 'pkgs <- c("likert","exact2x2","parameters","irr"); to_install <- pkgs[!(pkgs %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]; if(length(to_install)) install.packages(to_install, repos="https://cloud.r-project.org")'

# Run the analysis script (writes results/)
Rscript FuncConstructs-Statistics.r

# Collect the Table 3 outputs into a single reproducibility file
OUT=/workspace/repro.txt
echo "--- Table 3: GLMM textual summary ---" > "$OUT"
cat results/Table-3-RQ1-lambda.txt >> "$OUT"

echo "\n--- Table 3: Coefficients (with OR) ---" >> "$OUT"
cat results/Table-3-RQ1-lambda-coeff.txt >> "$OUT"

# Section 4: Formatting and submission block
echo '<artisan_submit>'
cat "$OUT"
echo '</artisan_submit>'

echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT

- BIC: 468.5
